title: Old, Middle and New Kingdoms
description: Egyptian history peaks in three kingdoms (Old, Middle, New), separated by Intermediate Periods when the country split.

facts.text: In the Oxford History of Ancient Egypt’s chronology, the Old Kingdom ran from about 2686 to 2160 BCE, the Middle Kingdom from about 2055 to 1650 BCE and the New Kingdom from about 1550 to 1069 BCE.
The Old Kingdom was the age of the great pyramids at Giza; the Middle Kingdom began when Egypt was reunited; in the New Kingdom Egypt became an empire.
Between the kingdoms came the First, Second and Third Intermediate Periods, when the land was politically divided, often under local rulers in Upper and Lower Egypt.

title: Three thousand years
description: Ancient Egypt lasted about 3,000 years, from unification around 3100 to 3000 BCE to Roman rule in 30 BCE.

facts.text: Ancient Egyptian civilization lasted about 3,000 years, from unification around 3100 to 3000 BCE until Egypt became a province of the Roman Empire in 30 BCE.
Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE: the Met dates unification to about 3100 BCE, and the Oxford History starts the First Dynasty about 3000 BCE.
Cleopatra, who died in 30 BCE, lived closer in time to the 1969 Moon landing than to the building of Khufu’s Great Pyramid, completed by the early 25th century BCE.

title: The Nile’s yearly flood
description: Summer rains in Ethiopia made the Nile flood Egypt each year, leaving fertile silt on fields in an almost rainless land.

facts.text: Egypt gets very little rain: a little over an inch a year at Cairo and less than an inch in Upper Egypt.
The Nile flooded Egypt each year, roughly from July to October, because of heavy summer monsoon rains far to the south in Ethiopia.
The Blue Nile, which rises in the Ethiopian highlands, plays the biggest part in bringing the Nile flood to Egypt.
As the flood drained away it left dark, fertile silt on the fields, a natural fertilizer that let Egypt support a dense population and prosperous cities.
A flood that was too low left some fields dry and could bring hunger; a flood that was too high could wipe out villages.
Egyptians believed the flood was a gift of the gods; if it was too great or too small, they blamed an angry river or a king who had neglected his duties, not the weather far to the south.

The Greek historian Herodotus, who visited Egypt in the 5th century BCE, called the Egypt the Greeks sailed to ‘the gift of the river’ (usually quoted as ‘the gift of the Nile’), meaning land built up by the Nile.

title: Black land, red land
description: Kemet, the narrow black land of the Nile valley, fed Egypt; Deshret, the red desert around it, was used for burials and guarded the borders.

facts.text: Egyptians called their country Kemet, ‘the black land,’ after the dark, fertile silt of the Nile valley.
Deshret, ‘the red land,’ was the Egyptian name for the hot, dry desert around the valley.
Between Cairo and Aswan, the Nile valley’s farmland is mostly 8 to 16 km wide, narrowing in places to a few hundred meters.
Egyptian cities could flourish only in the Nile valley, the Delta or desert oases, where people had water and good land.
The desert’s dry climate made it an ideal place for cemeteries.
Egypt had a favorable and secure location, bordered by deserts to the west and east, the Mediterranean Sea to the north and the First Cataract of the Nile at Aswan to the south.
Egypt was not isolated: it was a center for trade routes to and from western Asia, the Mediterranean and central Africa.

title: Farming by the flood
description: The Egyptian year ran in three seasons set by the Nile: flood, then plowing and sowing in the wet silt, then harvest and low water.

facts.text: The Egyptian year had three seasons of four months each: Akhet, the inundation; Peret, when the land emerged from the flood; and Shemu, when water was low.
When the floodwaters receded and left rich soil on the fields, planting and harvesting followed, then a dry season of low water until the next flood.
Egyptian farmers tilled with a wooden plow drawn by an ox or a donkey, and seed was sown from a funnel on the plow or trodden into the soil by sheep.
Egypt’s main crops were emmer wheat and six-rowed barley, along with lentils, beans, flax and onions.
Egyptian farmers cut their crops with sickles.
Early Egyptian farmers grew flax and wove it into linen.

title: The Nile as Egypt’s road
description: The north-flowing Nile and the north wind made a two-way road: drift north on the current, sail south with the wind, as far as the First Cataract.

facts.text: The Nile flows north through northeastern Africa into the Mediterranean Sea.
Egypt’s prevailing wind blew from the north, so boats going south, upstream, could sail with the wind behind them, while boats going north used the current and oars against the wind.
A wooden model riverboat from the tomb of the official Meketre at Thebes, from about 1985 BCE and now at the Met, shows twelve oarsmen rowing it downstream with the mast down.
The Nile was an important highway: the easiest way to travel, and essential for mining expeditions, trade, building projects and everyday travel.
The First Cataract at Aswan was a stretch of rock-strewn rapids that partly blocked the river, and it marked Egypt’s southern border.

title: The Two Lands
description: Egypt was two lands, Upper Egypt (the southern valley) and Lower Egypt (the Delta), each with its own crown, joined in the double crown.

facts.text: Upper Egypt was the southern Nile valley and Lower Egypt the northern Delta; the names follow the north-flowing river, so the south is upstream.
North of present-day Cairo, the Nile fans out into several branches, forming the Delta.
In late predynastic times, Upper Egypt and Lower Egypt were separate political lands.
The crown of Upper Egypt was white and cone-shaped; the crown of Lower Egypt was red and flat, with a rising back and a spiral curl in front.
Kings often wore the two crowns combined as the double crown, a symbol of Upper and Lower Egypt united under one king.
After unification, every Egyptian king held the title ‘King of Upper and Lower Egypt.’
No actual Egyptian royal crown has survived, so what the crowns were made of is not known for certain; we know them from works of art.

title: Egypt before the pharaohs
description: Farming villages appeared in Egypt by about 5000 BCE; Badarian potters and later towns followed, and Upper Egyptian culture spread north.

facts.text: By about 5000 BCE, villages in the Faiyum kept sheep, goats and pigs and grew emmer wheat, barley and flax.
Farming in Egypt only intensified after domesticated animals were introduced from Southwest Asia.
Around 4000 BCE, the Badarian farmers of Upper Egypt made thin-walled, well-fired, black-topped pottery that many regard as the best ever made in the Nile valley.
The Badarians also made ivory combs and spoons and flat stone palettes.
Before the kings, Egypt went from early farming communities to towns, and the culture of Upper Egypt spread north into Lower Egypt, probably through trade.
Boats are among the earliest designs painted on Egyptian Predynastic pots, which date to about 3500 to 3300 BCE.

title: Narmer and unification
description: Upper and Lower Egypt became one kingdom around 3100 to 3000 BCE. Tradition credits Menes; the Narmer Palette shows both crowns, but its meaning is debated.

facts.text: Egyptian tradition named Menes as the first king of unified Egypt, who joined Upper and Lower Egypt and founded Memphis, which became the capital.
Menes is legendary: scholars have tried, without settling it, to match him with early kings such as Narmer and Aha, and he may stand for several kings.
The Narmer Palette, a ceremonial palette found at Hierakonpolis in Upper Egypt and now in the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, shows Narmer in the white crown on one side and the red crown on the other.
The Narmer Palette dates to just before the First Dynasty and is one of the earliest examples of Egyptian relief sculpture.
Scholars disagree about the Narmer Palette: some read it as a record of Narmer conquering the north, others as a ritual statement of conquest rather than a real event.
Egypt’s political unity seems to have come gradually, through a shared culture and a series of conflicts over several reigns, rather than one single conquest.

title: Dynasties and dates
description: Egyptians counted years by reigns; Manetho grouped kings into 30 dynasties, which historians group into kingdoms. Dates before 664 BCE are approximate.

facts.text: Egyptians did not count years from one fixed starting point; they counted the years of each king’s reign.
The few surviving Egyptian king lists are broken in places, leave out some controversial rulers and list some rival dynasties as if they ruled one after another.
Around 300 BCE, the Egyptian priest Manetho wrote a history of Egypt in Greek that divided its rulers into 30 dynasties.
Manetho grouped kings into dynasties by factors such as family ties or the location of their main royal residence.
Manetho’s history survives only in fragments quoted by later writers, yet his 30 dynasties are still the basic framework of Egyptian history.
Historians group Egypt’s dynasties into larger periods: the Old, Middle and New Kingdoms and the Intermediate Periods between them.
Egyptian dates can be tied exactly to our calendar only from 664 BCE on; earlier dates are approximate, and different experts’ dates can differ by decades or more.

title: How the Nile made Egypt
description: River, flood, black land, guarding desert and the joining of two lands add up to one story of how Egypt began and why it lasted.

facts.text: Egypt’s favorable and secure location, guarded by deserts, sea and cataract, helped its civilization thrive for some 3,000 years.
